sentences.text: Eothoracosaurus was an extinct genus of eusuchian crocodylomorphs that lived in the Eastern United States during the Late Cretaceous.
Its name combines 'Thoracosaurus' with the prefix 'eos' for dawn, indicating it appeared earlier than its relative, while the species name refers to Mississippi.
This animal possessed a strongly elongated skull similar to the modern gharial, which grew notably broader towards the back of the head.
Preserved teeth were slender, conical, and fairly evenly spaced.
The frontal process of the nasal bone was twice as long as the main body, distinguishing it from Thoracosaurus where the ratio was closer to one to one.
The holotype, defined as the specimen the species is based on, consisted of a skull and postcrania discovered in 1931.
Christopher Brochu reexamined the material in 2004 and established the separate genus Eothoracosaurus due to substantial differences from other thoracosaurs.
Eothoracosaurus is associated with marine environments and coastal habitats, likely living in and around shallow marine areas.
It likely fed on fish and cephalopods.
Research by Boerman et al. (2026) interprets the endocranial anatomy as consistent with a marine ecology and a lack of capability for deep diving.
Eothoracosaurus is classified within the family Gavialidae.
It belongs to the class Reptilia.
The animal lived during the Campanian to Maastrichtian stages, from 83.6 to 66 million years ago.
Recent studies combining morphological, molecular, and stratigraphic data suggest that thoracosaurs like Eothoracosaurus were basal, non-crocodylian eusuchians rather than gavialoids.
